opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what you can actually learn from each case. When a model gets something wrong, there are usually a thousand different ways it could have failed. It might have misread the question, latched onto a spurious correlation, run out of capacity somewhere in the middle of a computation, or just been confused by something in the prompt. Failures are messy and kind of idiosyncratic, so even if you trace one failure carefully, it's not clear that tells you much about the next one.

When a model gets something right, especially something nontrivial like multi-step reasoning or a task it was never explicitly trained on, that's much more surprising. There has to be some mechanism inside the network that's actually doing the work. And mechanisms that work tend to be reused. If you can find the circuit or the representation that lets a model, say, track entities through a story or do variable binding, you've found something general, something the model relies on across lots of inputs. That's real knowledge about how the system computes.

There's also a practical side. If we want to trust these models, steer them, or know when they'll generalize, we need to understand the machinery behind their successes. Knowing why a model succeeds tells you the conditions it needs to keep succeeding, and it also tells you where the boundaries are. In a way, a good explanation of success gives you an explanation of failure almost for free: once you know the mechanism, you can predict the inputs that will break it. Going the other direction is much harder.

So I'd say success is where the structure is. Failure analysis is still useful for debugging, but if the goal is scientific understanding of what these models have learned, I'd much rather start with the things they do well and ask how that's even possible.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts messy, idiosyncratic failures with correct answers that reveal reusable mechanisms or representations, clearly presenting successes as more amenable to systematic explanation through internal mechanisms.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a bit of a contrarian position in interpretability, because a lot of the field got started by chasing failures. You find a weird behavior, a jailbreak, a hallucination, some bias, and you go dig into the model to figure out what went wrong. And that's useful work, I don't want to dismiss it. But I think it's actually the harder and less informative direction, for a couple of reasons.

The first is that failures are kind of unbounded. There are infinitely many ways to be wrong. If a model gets an arithmetic problem wrong, maybe it tokenized the number strangely, maybe it got distracted by something earlier in the context, maybe the circuit for carrying digits just didn't fire. Each failure is sort of its own little story, and when you explain one, it doesn't necessarily generalize to the next one. Whereas when a model gets something right, especially something it gets right consistently across a lot of inputs, there has to be some stable mechanism doing that. There's a real algorithm in there. And that algorithm is the thing worth finding, because once you have it, the failures often fall out for free. You can say, oh, the model implements this approximate procedure, and here are the inputs where that procedure breaks down.

The second reason is more philosophical, I guess. The interesting scientific question about these models isn't really "why are they bad," it's "how are they good at all?" We trained this thing on next-token prediction and it does multi-step reasoning, it translates languages, it follows instructions. Nobody wrote those capabilities in. So the success cases are where the actual mystery is. If I'm trying to understand what kind of computational object a language model is, I learn way more from a clean account of how it does something it wasn't explicitly built to do than from a postmortem on a mistake.

And there's a practical angle too, which is that explaining success gives you something to verify against. If I say "the model gets this right because of mechanism X," I can go intervene on X and check whether the behavior changes in the way I predicted. That's a falsifiable claim. Explanations of failure tend to be more narrative, like "the model got confused," and it's harder to turn that into an experiment.

So it's not that I don't care about failures. It's that I think the path to understanding failures runs through understanding successes first. You need the baseline of what the model is actually computing before you can say meaningfully where that computation went off the rails.

r001.rationale: The response says consistently correct answers rely on a stable internal mechanism or algorithm, while failures can have many distinct causes and may not generalize.

astra-6.text:
Because when a model gets something wrong, there are so many possible explanations. Maybe it doesn’t have the relevant information, maybe the question is ambiguous, or maybe it uses a strategy that just doesn’t work here. Explaining that failure can help us fix a particular problem, but it doesn’t necessarily tell us how the model does the task at all.

A correct answer gives you a more concrete puzzle: what computation made that success possible? Did the model recall an answer, pick up on a superficial cue, or actually carry out something like the reasoning we intended? Those can all produce the same output, but they imply very different behavior when you change the question.

So I’m interested in getting beyond ‘it got this right’ to understanding what we can trust that success to mean. If we can identify the mechanism and test whether the answer depends on it, we have a better basis for predicting when the model will succeed—and when it will fail.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the many possible causes of an error with the concrete question of what computation enabled a correct answer, and says identifying that mechanism helps explain the success.

sol-6.1.text:
Because getting an answer wrong is often less surprising than getting it right. A model can fail because it doesn’t know something, because the question is ambiguous, or because it uses a shortcut that breaks in that case. Finding a failure tells you something about its limits, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you how it works.

When it gets an answer right, the interesting question is: what computation actually produced that answer? Did it recall something it saw during training? Did it use a superficial pattern? Or did it combine information in a way that will generalize to a new problem? The same correct answer can come from very different mechanisms.

So I see explaining success as a way to understand the model’s capabilities and when we should trust them. If we know why a method works, we’re in a much better position to predict where it will stop working.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts wrong answers, which reveal limits but may not explain how the model works, with correct answers, whose underlying computation and mechanisms it says are worth investigating.
